summary: Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff worked in Indology and other fields. He studied at the University of Tübingen (~1793–1797) and held posts at the University of Tartu (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1814–1818), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw worked in Indology and history/archaeology. She studied at Leiden and Utrecht under Jan Gonda and others. She held posts at Utrecht, Groningen, Cambridge (1951–1959), and the University of Amsterdam (1958–1983).

Johanna Narten specialized in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. She studied at Saarland University and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg under Ernst Zinn and Karl Hoffmann, later serving as an Assistentin at Erlangen-Nuremberg (1973–1977).

Johannes Baunack was a scholar in linguistics and Indology. He earned his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig (~1873–1877) under Georg Curtius, Friedrich Zarncke, and Hermann Brockhaus, and later taught at Alte Nikolaischule (1878–1900).

Johannes Beltz works in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Lausanne, and EPHE under Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst, and held posts at Heidelberg University (1996–2001) and Museum Rietberg (2001).

Johannes Bronkhorst is an Indologist and scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He earned degrees from VU Amsterdam, Rajasthan, Pune (under S. D. Joshi), and Leiden. He held posts at Leiden, the Kern Institute, and Lausanne (1987–2025).
Johannes Brune was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Kiel University from 1903 to 1909, completing his Ph.D. under Hermann Oldenberg and Paul Deussen.

Johannes Edvard Lehmann worked in religious studies and Iranian/Central Asian studies. Educated at Copenhagen and Leiden under C. P. Tiele and M. V. Fausbøll, he held posts at Copenhagen, Berlin (1910–1913), and Lund University (1913–1928).

Johannes Friedrich was a scholar of linguistics and history/archaeology. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1911–1916) and later held academic posts at Leipzig (~1924–1950) and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1961).

Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis worked in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939) and later held posts at SOAS University of London (~1965–1981) and Leiden University (1978–1986).
Johannes Haeberlin was an Indologist. He studied at the Basel Mission in 1827 and at the Church Missionary Society College, Islington, in 1830.

Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who completed his Dr. phil. at Leipzig under Ernst Windisch. He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1920) before holding the chair of Indian philology at the University of Leipzig (1919–1937).

Johannes Klatt worked in Indology. He studied at Berlin and Halle under Albrecht Weber and August Friedrich Pott, subsequently working as an assistant, custodian, and librarian at the Royal Library of Berlin from 1872 to 1889.

Johannes Lohmann was a linguist and philosopher who earned his doctorate and habilitation in Berlin under Wilhelm Schulze. He held academic posts at Berlin, Basel, Rostock, and the University of Freiburg (1938–1963).
Johannes Mehlig was an Indologist. He studied under Paul Thieme (~1948–1953) and Friedrich Weller (~1950–1958).

Johannes Nobel specialized in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He studied under Heinrich Lüders at Berlin, where he also habilitated and taught, before holding the chair of Indology at the University of Marburg from 1928 to 1955.

Johannes Rahder worked in Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Leiden and Utrecht under Willem Caland and others, he held posts at Utrecht, Leiden (1931–1946), the University of Hawaiʻi, and Yale University (1947–1965).

Johannes Reinoud Abraham Loman was an Indologist. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Amsterdam under Adriaan Scharpé and Theodoor Paul Galestin, later holding a post at Leiden University from 1958 to 1973.

Johannes Schmidt worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, August Schleicher, and Albrecht Weber, subsequently holding professorships at the universities of Bonn, Graz (1873–1876), and Berlin (from 1876).

Johannes Schneider works in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Marburg, he held posts at Freie Universität Berlin, the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and the University of Munich (1999; professor from 2014).
